paragraphs: Say to him: tell us about your claim that God ordained two opposing schools. Do you mean in one place or in two different places? He cannot mean "one place," since it is impossible for two contradictory things to be commanded in one place at once. So he must mean: in two different places. Then ask him: in one time or in two times? Again, "one time" is impossible — for the same reason — so he must mean: at two different times. But the consequence of that position contradicts observed facts. The Children of Israel in the era of al-dawla (sovereign rule, the First Temple) celebrated each festival on a single day within the Holy Land; whoever travelled outside the Land would celebrate two days. Likewise outside the Land they would adopt all the practices of the Babylonians, and within the Land all the practices of the Palestinians. But this is contrary to current practice: the people of Shām — outside the Holy Land in the Diaspora — celebrate every festival as one day, except for Rosh Hashanah, which they take as two days. Those within the Land likewise take Rosh Hashanah as one day, like every other festival. So on Ibn Efraim's claim, God would have ordained three schools of festival-observance: one for those resident in the Holy Land (all festivals one day); one for the Palestinian Diaspora (one day except Rosh Hashanah, two days); and one for the rest of the world (two days for all festivals, except Yom Kippur).[{2}] And He must have commanded all three. A further consequence: a widow nursing a child who marries in Shām within less than two years and gives birth — that child must be legitimate in Shām by Shām's law, but bastard outside the Land by ʿIrāq's stricter law (which forbids the marriage). A child gestated whose mother was in niddah-state with relations less than seven days from the onset of bleeding — same problem. This whole thing makes a mockery of the claim that God ordained two different schools — whether at one time or at two.

Their contradicting themselves in these dressed-up sophistries: there are among them some muḥdathūn (late thinkers) who argue that the festival is two days by appeal to the narrative of Solomon. They say: 1 Kgs 8:66 reports that "on the eighth day he sent the people away"; and a parallel passage 2 Chr 7:10 reports that "on the twenty-third day of the seventh month he sent the people away." But the "eighth" of the seventh month would have been the twenty-second (counting from the fifteenth, the first day of Sukkot, plus seven). So clearly, on this reading, Solomon and the assembly took the eighth day as two days — the 22nd and the 23rd. So Solomon, in Jerusalem, took two days for the festival; and this contradicts Ibn Efraim's claim (which would have required one day in Jerusalem). Moreover: if Solomon and the people did take the festival as two days, the people of Shām have since abandoned the practice and reverted to one day. This whole argument is bahta (sophistic posturing) — a stratagem like the weaving of spiders, as Scripture says (Isa 59:5), "they weave the spider's web." It can further be said to him: if everything you have said were true, then someone outside Shām (in ʿIrāq) must, on Ibn Efraim's logic, adopt the Palestinian practice when traveling and take one day. Why, then, does a traveler from ʿIrāq who arrives in Shām take two days — i.e., according to his own country's practice? Two-day festival-taking is mandated, on his theory, outside the Land; but the traveler is in the Land. His own practice undoes his claim.

We then ask him about his claim of two textual-recensions: who told you both are right? Who claimed everything in either text is correct? Then ask him about (Isa 37:32): "for out of Jerusalem a remnant shall go forth" and Zech 14:4: "and his feet shall stand in that day on the Mount of Olives" — did God speak each verse to His prophet once, or twice? If he says "twice," we reply: then it must have been recorded twice — once with "of Hosts" or "in that day," and once without. But this is not in fact the case. Everything God said to His prophet by way of revelation was recorded once — the divergence in this matter is itself proof that God did not speak it twice in two ways. If, on the other hand, He spoke it only once, then in that one utterance either He said "of Hosts" or He did not. The one who said what He said is the right reading; the other is wrong — and ought not to be said.

Likewise put to him: take Mic 1:4 — "and ye shall flee through the valley of My mountains." Either God said wenastem ("and you shall flee") or wenistam ("and it shall be stopped up"). The difference of one letter (tav vs yod) produces opposite meanings. If God meant fleeing, no stopping-up applies; if He meant stopping-up, no fleeing applies. So the claim that God ordained both readings is categorically false.[{3}]

So too the disagreement between the Anbar and the Sūrā schools — among the Iraqis themselves: at Job 29:18, the Anbar reads "and like the sand I shall prolong my days" with one form; the Sūrā reads with another form (meaning a "bird" — the wushshān). On his claim that both are right, despite their being different, three readings must be divinely ordained. Enough! Likewise this binds him in every utterance God spoke to Moses (peace upon him) and the other prophets: in one of the languages, either Palestinian or Babylonian. Whichever it was, it was one — for it cannot have been said simultaneously. And it cannot have been the Babylonian, since that would entail that the Children of Israel — while in the Land — changed and corrupted the reading. Impossible: the transmitters of the reading among the Palestinians have transmitted it; so too the Byzantines and the Westerners (the Diaspora of the Second Temple); their reading is the Palestinian. If he says: then the Iraqis must have changed and corrupted it — we reply: that is exactly what we say. If he says: but in the Iraqis there were prophets like Ezekiel and Daniel — we reply: no one claims the recension changed in their day; the change came later, after the cessation of prophecy.

What can be said with confidence is this: when the community remained long in ʿIrāq and the surrounding territories of the Diaspora, their reading became Nabataeanized. We see that the reading of the people of ʿIrāq is close to the Nabataean speech. And every region's local Hebrew reading bends toward the prevailing local tongue. The people of the Ḥijāz and Yemen, for instance, cannot pronounce a fā-fricative (Hebrew ph) and instead say bā — because Arabic lacks the ph (their Hebrew "v"). Likewise they cannot pronounce gh — because Arabic lacks it; they substitute jīm. Similar phenomena in Bahrain. In Isfahan, the Hebrew reading sounds "non-Hebrew" because of the influence of Persian (the harshest tongue). In Byzantine territory, they fail to pronounce qamatz properly, because it does not exist in the local Romance tongue. Many local readers cannot pronounce gimel, because it is foreign to their local tongue. Many Iraqi Jews who grew up among the Nabataeans say daḥalū for dahalū, and so on, beyond enumeration. Who, then, can doubt — given all of this — that the Palestinian reading is the true one and is the one God spoke with His prophets? In the present age, no master of the Hebrew language and grammar — from Isfahan, Basra, Tustar, or elsewhere — fails to favor the Palestinian reading and pronounce it correct. Even those of the masters who only ever learned the Iraqi reading (knowing the Palestinian only by report) — when they discuss the language and grammar, they discuss it only on the Palestinian reading.

What we have said contains enough for one who seeks the truth. If someone asks how the additional letters in the Palestinian came to be dropped from all the Iraqi codices and on eastward to the farthest east — we reply: it is possible that the first copy that reached Shām[{4}] [from the East] contained errors; and that copies were then made from that copy with the errors carried forward, and the copies spread until they filled the world. Now let us turn to discussing what we ourselves hold concerning ijmāʿ (consensus) — clarifying our own doctrine — since we have promised that in the discussion of al-Fayyūmī, given that a number of our own companions have erred about it. ---
